title: A Cop Was Charged With Causing His Wife’s Miscarriage. Alabama’s Laws Came Down Harder on Pregnant Women Who Used Drugs.
author: Amy Yurkanin
content:
On the night of Feb. 15, 2022, Robert Maddox Jr., a rookie cop in a small
Alabama town, called his colleague in a panic. His wife was about three months
pregnant and bleeding heavily. They needed someone to watch their two sleeping
children while they went to the hospital.

Headland police Officer James “Bo” Knight arrived with his wife. He had been
serving as a mentor of sorts to Robert, who had just recently joined the
department, and had urged him to reach out if he ever needed help.

The situation Knight encountered was a heavy one. Robert had something in a
plastic bag that looked to Knight like fetal remains. His wife stood by
silently. Robert said he’d be back as soon as possible, that he was taking
both his wife and the bag to the hospital.

When the couple returned three hours later, Robert was holding a white
container.

“They put my fucking baby in a box,” he said.

Investigators soon began building a case that it was Robert who caused the
miscarriage. About six weeks after she lost the pregnancy, Brittany Maddox
reported her husband for assaulting her before and after she went to the
hospital. She first went to an abuse-prevention organization, which connected
her to the police and helped her get a protective order from the court. She
provided the Houston County judge with a description of how Robert choked and
beat her in front of their 1- and 2-year-old children just before the
miscarriage, as well as pictures taken starting the following week of marks on
her neck. She handed over text messages from Robert in which he promised not
to hurt her again and begged her to consider how his imprisonment would hurt
their family.

“Being honest is going to get us both screwed,” he wrote. “The truth is going
to give me locked up.”

Then, the Headland Police Department colleague who had offered to help Robert
stepped forward. Knight gave a sworn statement to investigators in Dothan, the
nearby city where the young couple rented an apartment. He recounted how,
weeks after the incident, Robert confided in him that he had hit Brittany in
the stomach, choked her and pushed her to the ground.

“I asked him how many times he has done this,” Knight said in his statement.
“He stated many.”

According to the statement, Knight asked when he had last hurt her — and
Robert responded “the night before you kept my kids.”

In Alabama, the legal implications of causing a miscarriage are severe.
Politicians and prosecutors have long proclaimed their mission to defend the
unborn. The state has gone further than almost every other to embrace “fetal
personhood” — the legal concept that embryos and fetuses deserve the same
rights and protections as children. The result is that people charged in
Alabama with harming a fetus face especially lengthy prison sentences.

The authorities came down hard on Robert, at least at first. He was charged
with murder.

But in the years that followed, Houston County’s criminal justice system would
prove lenient for him. Robert was released on bond about five weeks after his
arrest and never again saw the inside of a jail or prison cell.

His case stands in stark contrast to dozens of other fetal personhood
prosecutions in Houston County, which sits in the corner of the state near the
borders of Florida and Georgia. Those defendants were pregnant women. They
were charged not for actually harming their unborn babies but for potentially
endangering them — not by violence but by using drugs.

In all but one of those cases, which date back nearly two decades, their
babies survived. Some of the women spent months in jail and even went to
prison.

A former nurse, who had been battling a meth addiction for years, was arrested
in 2018 after she tested positive for drug use while in labor and wound up
spending nearly 10 months in prison. Another woman, who also tested positive
at the hospital where she gave birth, ended up in jail for four months in 2024
— and said many fellow inmates were women who’d been arrested for using drugs
while pregnant.

![A white woman with shoulder-length faded pink hair stands in a brightly lit
kitchen with wooden cabinets and floral
wallpaper.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20261031-Devine-Fetal-Personhood-
Dothan-032_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg)Courtney
Haney at a family member’s home last month in Dothan, Alabama. Her daughter
was born healthy, but Haney spent four months in jail for prenatal drug use.
A. Wallace for ProPublica

Houston County District Attorney Russ Goodman, who took office in January
2023, said in an email that his office has made efforts to help the women by
recommending addiction treatment as part of their sentences. He also said some
were rearrested and imprisoned for violating probation — or never completed
the treatment offered by the court.

“During my term it is rare that we would sentence a defendant in these types
of cases to a straight prison sentence,” Goodman said, “unless of course there
were other extenuating circumstances, such as prior criminal history.”

As for Robert Maddox, Goodman said that the evidence against him was
inconclusive, and he questioned the prior district attorney’s decision to seek
an indictment. “It pained me as a prosecutor that I was not to be able to seek
justice in this case,” he said.

Robert declined an interview but said in an email, “I was made out to be
someone I wasn’t.” He did not respond when pressed to elaborate. ProPublica
later sent him a detailed list of the allegations against him. He replied,
“That is not what happened.” In response to a follow-up email, he said his
wife had no bruising or marks at the hospital.

“If I was abusive and abused her then took her to the hospital they would have
saw the marks and not let me leave with her,” he wrote in an email.

Lourdes Rivera, president of the advocacy group Pregnancy Justice, said her
organization has identified [2,298
cases](https://www.pregnancyjusticeus.org/rise-of-pregnancy-criminalization-
report/) of women arrested since 2006 on charges related to their pregnancy.
Most of those were for drug use and are concentrated in Oklahoma, South
Carolina and Alabama. Rivera said the numbers of women prosecuted for
pregnancy loss appear to be [on the rise
](https://www.pregnancyjusticeus.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/Fall-2026-Data-Update.pdf)compared with the years
before the U.S. Supreme Court overturned the right to an abortion.

“Law enforcement is using laws that were never intended to apply to pregnancy
to investigate, arrest and punish women,” Rivera said. “And it’s only getting
worse.”

* * *

Robert’s promise not to hurt Brittany again after the miscarriage lasted about
a week, she said. She would later tell a judge that he began hitting and
choking her again, and photos from that time show bruising on her neck and
eye. In that time, something shifted.

“I started hating him when I saw my baby dead,” she wrote in response to
ProPublica’s questions.

She said it took her several weeks to come forward because she had to work
through complicated feelings about the loss of both her pregnancy and a
husband she still loved despite the hatred that was building. She also wasn’t
sure if she and her daughters could safely leave him.

About a week before she went to the authorities, she got a text from her
husband asking if she’d give him one more chance. “I can’t give you your baby
back,” he wrote. “That’s something I’m always going to live with knowing I did
that.”

For help in [English](https://www.thehotline.org/) or
[Spanish](https://espanol.thehotline.org/), call the National Domestic
Violence Hotline at 800-799-7233 or text “start” to 88788.

Asked about the text, Robert wrote to ProPublica, “I was referring to having
to pull my kid out a toilet I couldn’t believe I had to do that. It was
painful emotionally.”

Robert had started working as an officer at the Headland Police Department
about four months earlier. Brittany worried the other officers would side with
her husband, but she quashed her fears and reached out on social media to
several of them anyway. She said Robert went into her account and deleted the
messages she’d sent. But it was too late.

Knight, one of the officers she messaged, confronted Robert, who admitted that
he had hit Brittany in the stomach before the miscarriage, the officer later
told the Dothan police. Robert furiously messaged Brittany.

“If you want me to go to jail keep accusing me of it,” he wrote. “Just know I
love you and it will never happen again but I think I’m getting fired.”

Domestic abuse is a leading killer of pregnant women. And for every fatal
case, there are an estimated 70 nonfatal ones. Researchers have found that
[almost 13%](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38265064/) of women surveyed
experienced domestic violence during pregnancy.

Nonfatal cases usually go unreported, according to Maeve Wallace, an expert on
domestic violence at the University of Arizona. The same goes for
miscarriages, which often happen at home and may leave no medical record. That
can make it difficult to determine how often abuse causes miscarriage, she
said.

### Read More

[ ![](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/MIDV-
FINAL_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=459&h=306&crop=1) **These Women Were
Trying to Escape Domestic Abuse. ICE Detained Them Instead.**
](https://www.propublica.org/article/domestic-violence-immigrant-victims-ice-
detention)

Brittany said her relationship with Robert had been turbulent from the start.
She was still in high school when they started dating, and she uprooted her
life to relocate to his hometown of Dothan. She said he started physically
hurting her months into the relationship and that it escalated after the move.
Brittany found herself isolated in Alabama, where life revolved almost
entirely around her husband, two young children and the couple’s car-detailing
business.

“Robert would also hurt me if things weren’t done perfectly or if any issues
happened,” Brittany wrote.

Unlike many other victims of domestic violence, she hounded the police and
prosecutors to take her case seriously after the miscarriage.

Cases against abusers accused of causing pregnancy loss can be tricky to
prove, often requiring evidence that the abuser intentionally struck the
victim in the stomach and testimony from a forensic pathologist linking the
violence to the pregnancy loss. In one strange turn, a grand jury in a city
outside of Birmingham indicted a woman for starting a fight that led to her
being shot in the stomach and suffering a miscarriage.

It’s easier and more common to pursue charges against defendants when they are
accused of killing both a pregnant woman and her fetus.

Laws don’t provide an easy path for punishing abusers of pregnant women,
especially when the baby survives, according to law professor Mary Ziegler,
who teaches at the University of California, Davis. But laws do make
prosecution of pregnant women who use drugs astonishingly easy. Those cases
come to light almost automatically — and there is little opportunity to
challenge them. Hospitals frequently administer drug tests to pregnant women
and notify child protective services of positive results. Those agencies often
turn over that information to police in Alabama, where drug use is not grounds
just for a child welfare investigation but for a felony charge.

The women are prosecuted under Alabama’s chemical endangerment law, which
makes it illegal to expose children to drugs. Although the 2006 law initially
was designed to address the dangers of home-based meth labs, prosecutors
almost immediately began using it against pregnant women.

ProPublica identified more than 40 pregnant women arrested in Houston County
since 2009 on chemical endangerment charges after testing positive for drugs.
An analysis of court data also found that the county prosecuted women for
chemical endangerment at one of the highest rates in the state, though the
data doesn’t specify whether the cases involved pregnancies.

In one case, a 24-year-old whose newborn tested positive for methadone and
marijuana received a five-year prison sentence in 2009. Another woman, who’d
been convicted for exposing her fetus to THC in 2013, had her probation
revoked for possessing synthetic marijuana and spent about nine months in
prison.

Pat Jones, who was Houston County’s district attorney at the time of these
cases, did not respond to a request for comment.

According to Ziegler, there is a pronounced unevenness in who gets punished
under statutes that protect fetuses.

“The versions of personhood that are enshrined in our laws have tended to
focus on the conduct of women,” she said.

* * *

Courtney Haney grew up in Dothan but left at age 18 to join a high-pressure
sales crew that traveled across the country, selling boxes of frozen meat
door-to-door. The work was stressful, and it attracted misfits and risk-
takers. Several of her colleagues used drugs, but Haney became pregnant
unexpectedly and stayed clean.

Her daughter was born healthy, arriving exactly on her due date. But soon,
cracks appeared in her relationship with the father, and he split, taking the
baby with him. When her colleagues moved on to other cities, Haney remained in
Denver to look for her child. She had no family there and no friends. Her
despair became overwhelming. She turned to drugs and became homeless,
eventually losing custody.

Almost a year later, Haney found out she was pregnant again and returned to
Dothan in 2020 with a full-blown addiction to heroin. She went to the hospital
with contractions the week before she gave birth and knew she would test
positive for drugs. She also said no one offered her options for drug
treatment, even after she asked for help. Instead, hospital staff stabilized
and discharged her. She kept using until she returned to give birth, when she
was drug-tested again.

“I was holding my daughter in my hands and the police walked in,” Haney said.

They asked her questions, and she hoped they might show mercy and allow her to
go home with her child. After they told her she might be charged with a felony
for exposing her fetus to drugs, she burst into tears.

“I answered honestly, thinking that if I’ve answered honestly they wouldn’t
press charges,” she said. “And that was pointless.”

![A white woman with faded pink shoulder-length hair crosses her arms. She
wears a green T-shirt and lavender pants and stands in front of out-of-focus
vegetation. A tattoo on the back of her right hand reads
“Courtney.”](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/20261031-Devine-Fetal-Personhood-
Dothan-010_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg)To
avoid more criminal charges, Haney drove out of state to give birth to her two
younger children. A. Wallace for ProPublica

She was arrested for chemical endangerment three months later.

For women struggling with addiction during pregnancy, a chemical endangerment
arrest can initiate a cycle of devastating court fees, imprisonment on
probation violations and even additional charges. And the separation from
their newborns and other children can drive them deeper into addiction. Unlike
in many other counties, Houston County does not offer a drug court program,
which allows defendants to get substance-abuse treatment instead of prison
time and avoid a felony on their record.

A woman who was about seven months’ pregnant was arrested in Houston County
the very same day as Robert Maddox, in 2022. She was briefly jailed for
violating probation stemming from a past chemical endangerment conviction. She
then faced additional felony charges when, weeks later, she tested positive
for cocaine at the hospital where she gave birth. She later received a five-
year sentence and wound up at Tutwiler Prison for Women.

Her release date is right before Christmas in 2028.

Haney had no felony convictions, but a sentencing report recommended against
straight probation due to charges in other states that had been dismissed.
Ultimately, the Houston County district attorney’s office offered a plea deal
for a lesser charge and just over a year of probation.

Haney struggled to abide by the conditions of her sentence. She did not
complete court-ordered drug treatment and failed to report to her probation
officer several times. As a result, she was jailed for a total of four months.

Many of the other women jailed with her also had been arrested on charges of
chemical endangerment as a result of failing drug tests during childbirth.

“Whenever I went to jail, that’s where I met most of them,” Haney said.
“There’s a whole lot of them in Houston County.”

Haney became pregnant two more times while she was addicted. For her third
child, she traveled to nearby Georgia to give birth, and then to Florida for
her fourth. Neither state arrests women for prenatal drug use at the same high
rate as Alabama.

Xaviera Smith, a former nurse and mother of three from Tennessee, said she
knew she would be arrested before she even gave birth in Houston County to her
youngest son in 2018. Smith couldn’t deny the results of the drug test that
had been administered while she was in labor. She had been battling a meth
addiction for years.

She said that, fortunately, her baby was born healthy and did not need to go
to the neonatal intensive care unit for drug withdrawal.

Smith had a court-appointed attorney who negotiated a deal on her chemical
endangerment charge. She was sentenced to 10 years but could avoid prison by
serving time through the local work-release program.

“I just went to court and took what they gave me,” Smith said. ”There’s
nothing I really could do.”

After violating the terms of work release, she ended up in prison for nearly a
year.

* * *

Brittany Maddox believed the case against her husband was a straightforward
one. She felt there was solid evidence that the abuse caused her miscarriage.
But the effort proved to be harder than she anticipated.

A few months after his arrest, the grand jury declined to indict him for
murder, opting instead for a lesser charge of manslaughter.

The indictment alleged that Robert had “recklessly” caused the death of his
wife’s fetus by “punching her in the stomach with a closed fist.” The maximum
punishment would be 20 years in prison.

As Robert waited for his day in court, he asked the judge to relax some of the
conditions of his bond. He had lost his job with the Headland police because
of his wife’s claims of abuse and had started washing cars again. He wanted
the court to remove the ankle monitor so he could more easily travel to work
in Florida, which is near Dothan.

From her home out of state, Brittany had been calling the district attorney’s
office once or twice a month to ensure authorities kept an eye on her
estranged husband’s whereabouts. She was shocked to learn of his out-of-state
travel request — not from prosecutors but from a news story. For the first
time since his arrest, she felt unsafe.

A judge denied his motion to remove the ankle monitor but granted his request
to commute to north Florida.

Brittany stayed in touch with prosecutors and began to mentally prepare for
trial. She said that as months stretched into years, the conversations with
them began to shift. They asked her how she felt about a plea deal, and she
said she would be open to it, as long as the charge related to her miscarriage
wasn’t dropped completely.

“I told them I could push through a trial emotionally,” Brittany wrote.

Finally, almost four years after Robert was arrested, his attorney brokered a
plea deal with prosecutors. He would plead guilty to domestic violence, and
the prosecution would recommend  the manslaughter charge be dismissed.

Goodman, the district attorney, told ProPublica that he would not have been
able to prove at trial that Robert committed manslaughter. “There was never
any evidence that tied the actions of the defendant to the death of the baby,”
he said, adding that “no expert could tie a causal connection.”

He also said he explained to Brittany that “we would not have moved forward on
the manslaughter case” had he been in office when his predecessor chose to
seek an indictment against Robert.

Brittany said if Goodman believed the charge should be dropped, he should have
done it sooner, instead of having her spend years preparing for trial.

“The charge being dropped four years after he was arrested as part of a plea
deal makes no sense to me,” she said. “That wrecked me in a lot of ways, more
than the times I laid in bed for days after he hurt me.”

On May 18, 2026, Robert appeared before a judge in a Houston County courtroom.
Brittany attended the hearing as well. She had traveled to Alabama for all of
the hearings, even though she still feared being in the same room with Robert.

After all that waiting, the sentencing felt surprisingly short to her. When
the judge moved to dismiss the most serious charge, he didn’t say the word
manslaughter or mention the miscarriage. Brittany said she tried to ask
questions about the deal, but she wasn’t sworn in, and the judge quickly moved
on.

“The victim and the defendant were in a verbal dispute whereas the defendant
was alleged to throw the victim down and choke her,” the judge said. “The
state alleges that this occurred in front of their minor children as well.”

The judge went on to say that the presence of the children might have
increased Robert’s punishment to a minimum six months’ imprisonment. But
because he was a first-time offender, that minimum didn’t apply.

The judge sentenced him to five years’ probation and fined him about $3,000,
which he could pay off at $50 a month. Then the judge added one more thing:
anger management classes, to be completed through the court referral office.
